_note: Fictional sources for teaching: every source cited here, and every quotation from it, is invented. See sources.json.
title: Stormy with a chance of critics
context: An English literature student uses a critic's words in a paragraph about Emily Brontë's only novel.
question: Mark each part of the paragraph: is it the source's idea, the writer's own, or both (the writer building on the source)?
text: [[s1:Weather in {{i:Wuthering Heights}} is rarely just background: storms gather at moments of crisis, which invites the familiar reading of them as pathetic fallacy.]] [[s2:{{cite:lindgren2015|integral|page:88}} {{v:offers|offered}} a sharper version of this reading, arguing that Brontë uses storms {{q:not to mirror her characters' feelings but to release them}}.]] [[s3:The storm on the night Heathcliff leaves fits this well, since it breaks just as Catherine's distress becomes too great to contain.]] [[s4:Yet the calm weather of the closing pages is harder to explain in Lindgren's terms,]] [[s5:because stillness there seems to signal exhaustion rather than release, as if the story itself has finally run out of feeling.]]

s1.note: The writer's framing: an observation about the novel and a widely known way of reading it. It names no particular critic.

s2.note: Lindgren's argument, partly in her own words. The quotation is fitted into the writer's sentence so that it reads grammatically.

s3.note: The writer applies Lindgren's idea to a scene she doesn't mention. The idea is hers; the application is the writer's.

s4.note: The writer tests the source against the text. Mentioning Lindgren doesn't make this her voice: the judgement is the writer's.

s5.note: The writer's own reading, offered as an alternative to the source.

notes.text: In literary studies, short quotations woven into your own sentence are common — both from the novel and from critics. The skill is to make the quotation part of your argument, as s2 does, and then respond to it.
When the author is named in your sentence, APA and MLA put the page number straight after the quotation rather than next to the name.

chefsNote: A critic's words are seasoning. The reading is your dish.
